Q: Is scalar fmov guaranteed to clear the upper lanes to 0? A:

This documentation for the AArch64 architecture specifies that the semantics of the FMOV instruction, in its register-to-register variant, include:

var result : bits(128) = Zeros{};

which sets all 128 bits of result to zeros, and then:

result[0+:esize] = operand;

The +: is a slice operator, which is defined in ARM’s insanely formal specification of their specification language, Architecture Specification Language Reference. Quite simply, a+:b is a field of bits starting at bit number a, with a field length of b bits. So result[0+:esize] = operand; sets the first esize bits of result to the value of the instruction operand. esize is the number of bits for the data type of the instruction (16, 32, or 64 bits for half-, single-, or double-precision).

After that, the result is written to the destination register:

V{128}(d) = result;

So, all bits beyond the first esize bits are set to zero.

Q: How long does Apple's App Attest / DeviceCheck bit stay valid after the last token generation? A:

The two-bit storage is for a specific device, as you are using it, not for a certain duration until expiration.

See DEV blog on DeviceCheck:

https://dev.to/arshtechpro/devicecheck-and-app-attest-stopping-fraud-in-ios-apps-472e

Q: How to return the matched search string from multiple OR constraints within WHERE clause A:

You can use unnest(array(...)) and compare each pattern with column name

select table_name, column_name ,elem
from information_schema.columns t 
join lateral (
    SELECT elem FROM unnest(array['%price%','%parent%','%product%']) AS elem 
)p on column_name ILike elem
;

If columns patterns is a query parameter

select table_name, column_name ,elem
from information_schema.columns t 
join lateral (
    SELECT elem FROM unnest(STRING_TO_ARRAY('%price%,%parent%,%product%',',')) AS elem 
)p on column_name ILike elem
;

However, if the column name matches several templates, you will get several rows per column.

Aggregate by table_name, column_name

select table_name, column_name ,string_agg(elem,',') pattern
from information_schema.columns t 
join lateral (
    SELECT elem FROM unnest(STRING_TO_ARRAY('%price%,%parent%,%product%,%node%',',')) AS elem 
)p on column_name ILike elem
group by table_name,column_name
;

Q: Why is there no sorted_vector container in the C++ standard library, and what are the recommended alternatives? A:

The reason is that a sorted std::vector is easy to build with sort + lower_bound, but insertion/erase are O(n) and iterators/references can be invalidated. std::map gives different trade-offs, like stable iterators and cheap insertion/erase.

But as mentioned by Elijan9 in C++23, we actually got std::flat_map and std::flat_set, specifically for this use case.

For older standards, Boost flat_map/flat_set are the obvious alternatives.

Q: How to automatically approve/continue GitHub Copilot terminal commands in VS Code? A:

Update September 2026:

For individually managed VSCode installation, see the other answers, using approval on the developer side (like "chat.tools.global.autoApprove": true or "chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove": true).

But for those of us in the corporate world, since GitHub's September 2026 "enterprise-managed permissions for Copilot agent operations", a Copilot Business/Enterprise administrator can impose another permission layer which takes precedence over those user/workspace settings.

An enterprise administrator can classify agent operations as:

  • allow: execute without prompting;
  • ask: require a fresh human approval;
  • deny: do not allow the operation.

You can apply them to shell commands, file reads/edits and network domains.

For instance, an enterprise-managed copilot/managed-settings.json can contain rules such as:

{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Shell(rm -rf *)"
    ],
    "ask": [
      "Shell(git push *)"
    ],
    "allow": [
      "Shell(npm test *)",
      "Read(/src/**)"
    ]
  }
}

The important part for the OP is that those enterprise-managed permissions take precedence over the developer's VSCode auto-approval settings.

For example, even if the developer has "chat.tools.global.autoApprove": true, an enterprise-managed ask rule for Shell(git push *) still requires a fresh approval for each matching operation.
GitHub explicitly states that a managed ask rule cannot be bypassed by an auto-approval setting, a previously saved approval, bypass mode, a hook, or another approval shortcut.

An administrator can go further with permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable": in VSCode, that turns chat.tools.global.autoApprove off entirely and prevents the user from re-enabling it(!).

An administrator can also use allow rules to let selected command families execute without repeatedly prompting developers, while still requiring confirmation for more sensitive commands.

Warning: As soon as the enterprise defines an allow list, that list describes the operations that may run automatically. Other supported operations fall back to requiring approval unless another managed rule says otherwise. (in other words: "whitelist")

And when multiple rules apply, the precedence is:

deny > ask > allow

The granular rules apply to VSCode Copilot sessions using Agent Host. GitHub also supports the managed-permissions mechanism in Copilot CLI and the GitHub Copilot app.

This is different from the existing answers in another respect: it only addresses permission prompts for agent operations.

The OP's second issue is still separate:

Automatically continue iterations when working on complex problems

Settings such as chat.agent.maxRequests, as mentioned in the other answers, control how long the agent can continue before asking to proceed.
Enterprise-managed allow/ask/deny rules do not replace that setting.

So, as of 2026, there are really two levels:

VSCode/user settings
    |
    +-- global or command-specific auto-approval

Enterprise-managed Copilot permissions
    |
    +-- allow / ask / deny
    +-- can prevent global auto-approval entirely

If Copilot is not enterprise-managed, the existing chat.tools.global.autoApprove answer remains the simpler and more direct solution.
If it is enterprise-managed, local auto-approval only works within the limits imposed by the enterprise policy.
